Where does global inequality lie: between or within countries?
Triangulating between the two main data sources: the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform, and the World Inequality Database.

Joe Hasell · Oxford Martin School, Our World in Data
Pablo Arriagada · Our World in Data
Bertha Rohenkohl · Our World in Data

slides.notes:
SHORT TALK — 15 min, academic audience (inequality researchers). Aim to talk for 12-13 min so Q&A can happen.

Abstract / opening framing:

Where does global inequality lie: between or within countries? Despite a new wealth of data, we're still in the dark: PIP survey data says 'mostly between', WID/DINA says 'mostly within'.

The divergence mixes known measurement problems with differing methodological choices. That has left unexplored what is arguably the most attractive vantage point of all, lying between these two worlds of measurement: one anchored to a traditional ‘survey income’ concept, while allowing for underestimation at the top. Recent expansion of both datasets makes such bridging far more feasible than it used to be. Seen from such a triangulated vantage point, the between/within split looks close to even.

Running order: framing → why now (coverage + DINA) → Q2 walkthrough (between/within) → one ask for the room about OWID.

Expectation-setting slide, placed before the problem setup.

Says up front what the talk is not, so the contribution claim is honest: the value is in re-presenting existing work clearly, not in new data or new method.

(Notes to fill in — Joe's framing.)

slides.notes:
Setup slide. ~60-75 seconds.

The two main sources answer the same question in opposite ways, and both are respectable. Left: WID/DINA, between-country has fallen to about a third of the total. Right: the World Bank's own flagship report, on PovcalNet (the ancestor of PIP), where between-country is about two-thirds.

Note for questions: this is not a clean apples-to-apples gap. It mixes (i) the data source, (ii) the inequality index (Theil/GE(1) on the left, mean log deviation/GE(0) on the right), (iii) the year, and (iv) the income concept. That is the point of the talk: the headline disagreement bundles measurement problems together with methodological choices. In both figures the warm colour is between-country, which helps when pointing at them.

Where does global inequality lie: between or within countries?
Summary

• Despite a new wealth of data, the question is wide open: 
    • PIP (survey data) says mostly between — (Milanovic ; Milanovic & Lakner)
    • WID (DINA) says mostly within (Chancel & Piketty, 2021)
  • Divergence due to a mix of: 
    • Known measurement problems (top incomes; data gaps — mix of income/consumption survey data) 
    • Differing methodological choices (source data, adjustments/assumptions, welfare/income concept)
      • -> Two 'worlds' of measurement 
-------
  • Exploring the 'center ground': anchored to traditional survey income concepts, while addressing concerns about their accuracy (Nolan... Morelli...)
  • Recent expansion of PIP and WID datasets makes 'bridging' between them more feasible
  • Seen from a center-ground perspective, the between/within split looks closer to 50/50.

blocks.html: What do we know about global income inequality?
Overview

• Three basic questions
  • About the two sources: PIP and WID
  • Q1: Is income inequality rising basically everywhere? (PIP: No; WID: Yes)
  • Q2: Which is bigger: inequality between countries, or within countries? (PIP: Between; WID: Within)
  • Q3: Who are the richest 1% in the world?

slides.notes: The raw comparison, before any bridging adjustments. Top: P10/P90/mean for three countries on a shared log scale - WID (pre-tax national income, per adult) left, PIP (disposable income/consumption, per capita) right. Bottom: MLD level decomposition (between vs within) computed on just these three countries. Data pipeline: data/scripts/10_fig_raw_comparison.py

blocks.html: Q2: Which is bigger: inequality between countries, or within countries?

slides.notes: Pedagogical anatomy of the MLD decomposition, using the slide-12 pair (WID pre-tax per adult vs PIP) and the three highlight countries. Key intuition: on a log income axis, each person's log-gap to the overall mean is a visible distance that splits exactly into the between gap (their country's mean to the overall mean, dark) and the within gap (them to their country's mean, light). The stacked bar is the population-weighted average of those gaps. Data: data/scripts/12_fig_mld_decomp_explainer.py.

blocks.html: Q2: Which is bigger: inequality between countries, or within countries?

The mean log deviation is the population-weighted average of everyone’s log-distance from the overall mean μ — and it splits exactly into a between-country and a within-country part:

MLD = Σi wi ln(μ / xi)  =  Σc wc ln(μ / μc)
BETWEEN + Σc wc MLDc
WITHIN  — wc = population share; MLDc = inequality inside country c

slides.notes: Build-up: two bridging steps between the raw WID series and PIP. Step 1: per-adult -> per-capita basis. Step 2: pre-tax -> post-tax national income. Between-country share of MLD climbs 28% -> 36% -> 49%, vs PIP's 76%. Same component and data as the previous slide - the sources prop selects the columns (data/scripts/10_fig_raw_comparison.py). Added: PIP top-adjusted (WID post-tax shape grafted above the p99-99.1 bin, anchored at PIP's level there; splice point parameterized in data/scripts/10_fig_raw_comparison.py). PIP_consinc is a PLACEHOLDER column (ghost) for the future consumption->income adjustment; data source identified: garden/wb/2026-06-26/world_bank_pip/percentiles (income+consumption percentiles for 88 country-years).

blocks.html: Q2: Which is bigger: inequality between countries, or within countries?

slides.notes: Explainer for the consumption->income adjustment behind the PIP_consinc bridging column. Model: per-percentile OLS ln(y_p) = alpha_p + beta_p ln(c_p), fitted on PIP's 88 dual country-years (19 countries; no SSA/South Asia - out-of-sample transfer caveat). Dropdown covers all 123 consumption countries; * marks the 18 dual ones where the actual income series overlays as a fit check. Scripts: 04_fit_consinc.py (fit), consinc.py (series), 13_fig_consinc_explainer.py (this figure).

blocks.html: Q2: Which is bigger: inequality between countries, or within countries?

Putting PIP’s consumption countries on an income basis: for the 88 country-years where PIP publishes both income and consumption distributions, we fit one regression per percentile, ln yp = αp + βp ln cp, and apply the fitted mapping to every consumption-based country. Income countries are unchanged.

slides.notes: Top adjustment explainer, CHAINED method (2026-08-11): base = PIP_consinc (income basis), splice P95 (anchor p94-p95, first adjusted bin p95-p96). Chart shows consumption (observed), income basis (imputed), and top-adjusted; income countries show two lines. Scripts: topadj.py, consinc.py, 11_fig_topadj_explainer.py. Default country: Indonesia.

blocks.html: Q2: Which is bigger: inequality between countries, or within countries?

How the top-adjusted series is built: starting from the income-basis series (previous slide), everything below P95 is kept as is. Above P95, incomes are assumed to follow the shape of WID’s post-tax distribution, anchored at the P94–95 value: adj(Py) = inc(P94–95) × WID(Py) / WID(P94–95). This is an additional step on top of the consumption→income adjustment: the bottom 95% is untouched; the top 5% — and hence the mean — is reshaped.

slides.notes: The same bridging chart, now computed over the WHOLE common sample: all 211 countries covered by both PIP and WID (not just the three example countries). Same component (fig-raw-comparison, bars-only mode: no lollipops in the data), same methods and parameters as the three-country version — the only change is the country set. The rescaled WID series takes its means from PIP_topadj (the far end of the PIP-side chain), so its between component equals PIP top-adjusted's exactly — the bridge meets in the middle. Between-share ladder: WID pre-tax/adult 21.5% -> per-capita 27.7% -> post-tax 38.2% -> at adjusted PIP means 41.7% -> PIP top-adjusted 55.5% -> PIP cons->income 60.4% -> PIP 69.2%. Data: data/scripts/14_fig_bridging_all.py.

HOW TO EDIT
Slides are data, not markup

• Every slide lives in content/slides.json — the single source of truth.
  • Text blocks hold HTML; component blocks reference interactive modules by name.
  • Claude edits the JSON and drops component files into components/; you edit the same JSON through the point-and-click editor.
  • Both authoring paths converge on one file, so nothing gets clobbered.

slides.notes: The key architectural idea: because slides are data, programmatic edits (Claude) and manual edits (the inline editor) are just two writers of the same JSON.
